name: New Caledonia
summary_text: New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while the territory legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are therefore French national provisions that apply here as French law, and no source in this inventory records a local ordinance narrowing them. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.  Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on the first same-sex wedding solemnised in France under that law. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the French government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.  Sexual identity became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code through the sexual-harassment legislation of 2012, which enabled prosecution of discrimination and of transphobia as discrimination; the provision was amended in 2016 to read gender identity. As French law, the provision reaches New Caledonia.  Placement of detainees follows the legal gender marker rather than anatomy: Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code assigns incarcerated trans people according to their recorded sex, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by other detainees (BuzzFeed News, 12 January 2018). The French prison framework governs the collectivity's establishments in the same way.  France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of the rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. Because French law applies here, the opinion extends to establishments in New Caledonia.

sources.title: 2014 study on overseas acceptance + 2013 parliamentary vote breakdown for New Caledonia deputies
sources.documents: Documents New Caledonia-specific climate: only ~20% of overseas residents saw homosexuality as sexuality like any other vs 77% metropolitan; acceptance lower where religion/family honour prominent; first same-sex marriages in Saint Martin/French Polynesia caused demonstrations; 2 New Caledonia deputies voted for same-sex marriage; article notes LGBTQ people in New Caledonia widely accepted with large nightlife/dating scene, more notable in South Province than Kanak-majority North Province.

name: Nicaragua
summary_text: Nicaragua does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or trans identity. Article 204 of the Criminal Code, inserted by religious legislators into a bill originally drafted to protect women from rape and signed into law in July 1992, made it an offence punishable by up to three years' imprisonment to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner"; the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality challenge in March 1994. The provision's vagueness had also made it usable against LGBT-rights organising and sexual-health work. Its language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008, and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since.  Formal legality does not translate into protection. The US State Department's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices in Nicaragua documents a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived opponents of the government that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among the year's significant human rights violations. The official US assessment places anti-LGBTI abuse inside a broader climate of state impunity.  Amnesty International's May 2019 reporting places homophobia inside that same repression. The crackdown on protests that began in April 2018 left at least 325 people dead and more than 2,000 injured, according to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, and journalist Miguel Mora described being beaten by a pro-government mob and being targeted partly for being gay.  Documented violence against LGBT people is persistent and under-recorded. A 2012 Center for Justice and International Law survey counted 53 aggressions between 1999 and 2011, among them 15 murders: 10 gay men, 4 transgender people and 1 lesbian, with the true total expected to be higher. The NGO Programa Feminista La Corriente reported 67 assaults, 1 hate crime or murder and 2 suicides in 2021; 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes and 1 suicide in 2022; 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults and 1 extortion in 2023; and 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes and 1 missing person in the first two quarters of 2024. Trans women are the most targeted group, and state police are among the aggressors, tied with family members in 2022. Attacks go largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes.  Family-law exclusion is explicit. The Family Code approved by the Nicaraguan Congress in June 2014, in force from 8 April 2015, limits marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples, and Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples. Several organisations filed an action of unconstitutionality against the Code. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that parties to the American Convention on Human Rights must grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration rights including marriage, and no Nicaraguan implementation is recorded.  Discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is barred in several settings, including health care. Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 bars discrimination in access to health services on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, which is the provision most directly relevant to a visitor seeking care.  Public opinion is largely opposed. A Pew survey conducted from 9 November to 13 December 2013 found 77% opposed to same-sex marriage, 16% in favour and 7% unsure, while the 2017 AmericasBarometer showed 24.5% support.
